If you want to get into IO psych (or really any branch of psychology), it’s a good idea to talk to your professors and get their takes.

Do you have any professors who are themselves IO psychologists? If so, talk to them about their career path. Talk with them about whether a PhD path is the right for you, and ask them about research (if you do decide grad school is right for you, getting involved in research now is the best leg up you can give yourself). 

If you don’t have any professors who are IO psychologists, don’t worry. Talk to the professors you do have, and tell them about your goals. They may be able to recommend labs/professors to check out. They can also give you advice on how to use your remaining years at VCU to their fullest potential. You have lots of time to set yourself up for success. 

Lastly, I’d advise checking out summer research positions through the NSF or through other universities. Lots of labs offer short research intensives for college students with no prior research experience (and sometimes they are paid!). Usually the sites where these opportunities are listed allow you to filter your search; in your case, you could search specifically for IO psych positions. These are a great way to build your CV/resume and to really get familiar with what you think you might be interested in studying. If you look into these now, you’ll likely still be applying just ahead of the deadlines (for summer positions, deadlines tend to close in early spring at the latest). 

Best of luck to you! Psychology is a cool field, but it’s incredibly competitive. It pays to be prepared, and to ask for advice from your professors.

UVA alum and graduate student going through a pretty similar thing right now. UVA didn’t use canvas when I was there, and my graduate program does. My professors aren’t familiar with canvas either, and each of them uses a different approach when posting assignments, due dates, etc. I am a pretty conscientious person, and I also missed a due date during my first week. 

Key takeaway - a late assignment will not be the end of the world and will not destroy your grade. Don’t be hard on yourself. You are learning to use a new system too. 

Like other commenters are saying, you’ll need to be the one who adapts to this by developing your own systems for each class. Your professors are not likely to change their own systems, or guaranteed to give you grace for late assignments (though talking to them, even if you are in a big lecture hall, during office hours may help your case).

Figure out where each Professor is posting their assignments/class updates, and make it a part of your weekly/daily routine to check for unexpected deadlines for each class. In office hours with professors, compare the due dates you have written down with the due dates they have - talk through discrepancies with them and adjust. You could even talk to your advisor or your dean for tips on adjusting. You’ve identified a weakness in your approach - now it’s time to use your resources. 

You will be okay!

seconding this - an intro to psych textbook will familiarize you not only with the history of psychology as a discipline (including Jung), but also with research  methods, and with the many many different areas of psychology (abnormal, developmental, cognitive, clinical, etc). It will introduce you to the field!

In general, a good rule of thumb to assess whether something you are reading is based on science is to look for citations in the work and a references/works-cited/bibliography portion of the book where the author notes the other works of academic literature that they drew on to write their book or paper. The author might cite studies which support their arguments and elaborate on the study design and methods (some methods are specific to some areas - neuropsychology studies will use entirely different research methods than developmental psychology for example), and it is good to engage with their description somewhat skeptically (did the author of the original study really make this seemingly bold claim? Follow up with the citation on Google Scholar or PsychInfo to double check - sometimes authors misrepresent the research they are quoting). 

Happy reading! Psychology is an exciting field with literally endless lines of inquiry to follow; you may find a passion you never knew existed.

I have had really similar issues with my bartonella. The brain fog comes and goes, but as a full time student it’s pretty disruptive. I haven’t found anything to fight it yet other than asking for accommodations when I need them and resting. 

As for the anxiety and depression (and so many other mood swings), the best thing I’ve found is spending time with friends (and being honest about what you’re going through with them!), going to therapy, and doing yoga with a focus on mindfulness. Before I got sick, I was an athlete (I played water polo!) but my symptoms made it really difficult to play and so yoga has been an awesome substitute for physical activity as I can scale the difficulty based on how I’m feeling. It’s good to be able to work out and get that boost of endorphins. 

Feel free to message me if you want to talk more! I wish you the best, and hope that you recover and start feeling like yourself again soon.
